'''Peyton Williams Manning''' (born March 24, 1976) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 18 seasons. Nicknamed "'''the Sheriff'''",<ref>{{Cite web |last=Dator |first=James |date=January 25, 2016 |title=Why is Peyton Manning's Nickname "The Sheriff" |url=https://www.sbnation.com/lookit/2016/1/25/10826002/peyton-manning-broncos-nickname-the-sheriff-cam-newton-panthers-super-bowl |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210308154244/https://www.sbnation.com/lookit/2016/1/25/10826002/peyton-manning-broncos-nickname-the-sheriff-cam-newton-panthers-super-bowl |archive-date=March 8, 2021 |access-date=January 26, 2016 |website=[[SB Nation]]}}</ref> he spent 14 seasons with the [[Indianapolis Colts]] and four with the [[Denver Broncos]].<ref name="nydailynews2007">{{Cite web |last=Begley |first=Ian |date=March 25, 2007 |title=Peyton stars on 'SNL' |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/2007/03/25/2007-03-25_peyton_stars_on_snl_.html |url-status=dead 2007 |website=[[New York Daily News]]}}</ref> Manning is considered one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time.<ref name="Greatest"/> A member of the [[Manning family|Manning football dynasty]], he is the second son of former NFL quarterback [[Archie Manning]], older brother of former NFL quarterback [[Eli Manning]], and uncle of [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]] quarterback [[Arch Manning]].<ref>{{cite web | last=Bardahl | first=Jayna | title=Peyton Manning details nephew Arch's 'huge advantage' entering first season as Texas starter | website=The Athletic | date=July 1, 2025 | Volunteers football|Tennessee Volunteers]], winning the [[Maxwell Award|Maxwell]], [[Davey O'Brien Award|Davey O'Brien]], and [[Johnny Unitas Golden Arm Award|Johnny Unitas Golden Arm]] awards as a senior en route to victory in the [[1997 SEC Championship Game]].

Manning was selected [[List of first overall National Football League Draft picks|first overall]] in the [[1998 NFL draft]] by the Colts and served as their starting quarterback from 1998 to 2010. He helped transform the struggling Colts franchise into consistent playoff contenders, leading them to 11 playoff appearances, eight division titles, three [[AFC Championship Game]]s, two [[Super '''Peter Nicholas Boulware''' (born December 18, 1974) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[linebacker]] for nine seasons with the [[Baltimore Ravens]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He played [[college football]] for the [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State Seminoles]], earning recognition as a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]].  A first-round pick of Baltimore in the [[1997 NFL draft]], he played his entire pro career for the Ravens.

Boulware was a [[Republican party (United States)|Republican]] candidate for the [[Florida House of Representatives]] in the 2008 general election.

'''Peter L. Warrick''' (born June 19, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] for six seasons in [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for [[Florida State Seminoles football|Florida State Seminoles]] where he was consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors twice and won the 1999 National Championship with the team and was the named Sugar Bowl MVP. '''Peter Nicholas Duranko'''<ref>[https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/D/DuraPe20.htm "Pete Duranko profile" ''pro-football-reference.com''] August 14, 2011</ref> (December 15, 1943 – July 8, 2011) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive end]] for the [[Denver Broncos]] of the [[American Football League]] (AFL) and [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Notre Dame Fighting Irish football|Notre Dame Fighting Irish]]. Duranko was an [[All-America college football team|All-American]] and a member of Notre Dame's 1966 national champion team. He was selected by the Broncos in the [[1966 American Football League draft|1966 AFL draft]] and was also chosen by the [[Cleveland Browns]] in [[1966 NFL draft|the NFL draft]]. He played in 98 games for Denver in an eight-year career from 1967 through 1974.  After sitting out the 1975 season due to injury, he was one of the first free agent signings of the NFL's expansion [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] on January 27, 1976, however, he did not make the roster and was released by the Buccaneers on July 18, 1976, before the franchise played its first preseason game.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.prosportstransactions.com/football/Search/SearchResults.php?Player=duranko|title= "Pete Duranko search" ''Pro Sports Transactions'' |accessdate=6 Sep 2024}}</ref>

At [[Bishop McCort High School]], he played [[High school football|football]], ran [[Track and field|track]], and was a [[shot put]]ter. '''Peter Kornel Gogolak''' ({{IPAc-en|lang|ˈ|ɡ|oʊ|ɡ|ə|l|æ|k}}; '''{{langx|hu|Gogolák Péter Kornél}}'''; born April 18, 1942) is a Hungarian-born former [[American football]] player who was a [[placekicker]] in the [[American Football League]] (AFL) for the [[Buffalo Bills]], and in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for the [[New York Giants]].<ref name=syrc>{{cite news |url=http://www.syracuse.com/kirst/index.ssf/2015/10/the_bills_the_giants_and_a_legendary_link_kicker_pete_gogolak_still_follows_both.html |newspaper=Post-Standard |location=Syracuse, New York |last=Kirst |first=Sean |title=Pete Gogolak: A 'sidewinding' bridge from New York to Buffalo  |date=January 23, 1991 |access-date=March 24, 2016 }}</ref>

Gogolak is widely considered the chief figure behind the game's adoption of [[Field goal (football)#Soccer style|soccer style placekicking]].<ref name=ctribhrev>{{cite news |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1987/12/27/hungarian-revolution-plays-role-in-revolutionalizing-kicking-game/ |newspaper=Chicago Tribune |agency=Knight Ridder |last=Spencer |first=Clark |title=Hungarian Revolution plays role in revolutionalizing kicking game |date=December 27, 1987}}</ref> In 1966, after playing two seasons for the AFL's Bills, he joined the NFL's Giants in May after playing out his option,<ref name=gsgogoaow>{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=Y140AAAAIBAJ&sjid=GJsEAAAAIBAJ&pg=5091%2C2949224 |newspaper=Tuscaloosa News |location=Alabama |agency=Associated Press |title=Giants sign Pete Gogolak; all-out war? |date=May 18, 1966 |page=15 }}</ref><ref name=lewsgg>{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=TmogAAAAIBAJ&sjid=3GYFAAAAIBAJ&pg=2653%2C2185005 |newspaper=Lewiston Daily Sun |location=Maine |agency=Associated Press |last=Hand |first=Jack |title=Giants sign Bills Pete Gogolak; move could provoke pro grid war |date=May 18, 1966 |page=13 }}</ref> sparking the "war between the leagues" and effectively expediting the subsequent [[AFL–NFL merger]] agreement in June. He is distinguished as being the first [[Hungarians|Hungarian]] to play in the NFL. His younger brother [[Charlie Gogolak]] also became a placekicker, playing six seasons professionally.

In 2010, the New York Giants announced that Gogolak would be included in the team's new Ring of Honor to be displayed at all home games in their new stadium.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.giants.com/news/headlines/story.asp?Story_Id=44384 |title=Headlines - Story - Pete Gogolak Inducted to Ring of Honor - Giants.com |access-date=2010-10-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100930110416/http://www.giants.com/news/headlines/story.asp?Story_Id=44384 |archive-date=2010-09-30 |url-status=dead }}</ref>  To this day, he remains the Giants all-time leading scorer with 646 points.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/nyg/ | title=New York Giants Team Records, Leaders, and League Ranks | website=[[Pro-Football-Reference.com]] }}</ref>

'''Peter Samuel Pierson''' (born February 4, 1971) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]] for eight seasons with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] and one for the Indianapolis Colts of the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Washington Huskies football|Washington Huskies]] and was selected by the Buccaneers in the fifth round of the [[1994 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1994 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1994/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-31 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

Pierson was released by the Buccaneers as a rookie in 1994, and was signed by the [[Kansas City Chiefs]]. After spending approximately one week one the Chiefs practice squad, he was subsequently re-signed by the Bucs. He remained with the Bucs for the season, but did not play in any games (spending part of the time was on the Bucs' practice squad).

Pierson spent the 1995 season as a backup right tackle (12 games, four starts), but moved mainly to the left side when the Bucs hired [[Tony Dungy]] in 1996. Playing behind one of the NFL's upper echelon left tackles, [[Paul Gruber]], Pierson played in 57 games with two starts from 1996 to 1999.

When Gruber suffered a broken left leg in the season finale of the 1999 season, Pierson started the Bucs' playoff contests versus the Washington Redskins and the NFC Championship game versus the St. Louis Rams.  He started 15 games in 2000 at left tackle.

In 2001, Pierson shared time in 15 games at left tackle. Pierson was released by the Bucs in August 2002. He signed with Dungy and the Indianapolis Colts, and appeared in two games as a reserve in his final NFL season.

In his nine-year career, Pierson appeared in 121 games and made 21 starts.
